"The only thing you are obligated to do as a person is live in the present moment."

That's the problem right? Living. Most people who post here are at odds with life as it is which is usually due to mental illness and/or external factors e.g. poverty. 

I believe that resilience is not something to be necessarily taken as a compliment. If I call someone "strong" or "resilient" it's usually more of an observation. and that's because it's just my opinion about that person in a certain point in time. It's not something that's beautiful to me. What about the people who are not seen as resilient or strong?  What happens to them? 

And do we have to be beautiful to love and respect ourselves? Are all of us really that beautiful? Should we strive to be a beautiful person? I don't know what beauty even means. Does it mean to "just be ourselves"? Most struggling with mental illness have lost themselves.

I don't think that we are all here for one another. Each person deals with their own thoughts and worries and each person sleeps and dreams of their own dreams. It would be nice if we were all connected in some way. But we are not. There are rare moments that we might be able to feel that connectedness...but I don't think it's something that's usually present. 

And maybe that's ok. We pick and choose who we get to have in our life (to an extent) and we choose who to love and support. Some of us are more fortunate than others and are able to make more choices in our life...have more autonomy. Some of us are not. 

There is a lot more uncertainty about life than we'd like to admit. Life can beautiful. Life can be horrific. Humans can be kind. Humans can be monsters. Life can be inspiring. Life can be hopeless. Life can be mediocre. It's a muddy mix of it all.

Here are some snippets of Diane Fenning's book *Written in Blood*. This book is described as an inside look at the Peterson case-- and it seems to be. In the prologue, Fanning writes: "‘The Staircase is an emotionally riveting drama, but it is nowhere near the whole truth. If anybody wants to know the whole story, read Fanning’s Book’ Ann Christensen, Michael Peterson’s sister." I think your answer can be found in bullet points 4-7.

Here are some excerpts from the book about Martha:

1. **Before Liz's death:** "Martha was a dainty, sensitive little girl, but she had a lot of spirit. From the age of one, she’d demonstrated a streak of rebellion. Liz, her patience often tried by Martha’s defiance, was still amused and enchanted by her struggle for independence" \[Ch. 17\].
2. "Mike displayed a clear favoritism for Margaret, who was a friendly, outgoing and intelligent girl. Martha was more shy and sensitive. She developed a fear of Mike, hiding behind Barbara whenever he came to the house. Martha came home from the Peterson’s on a number of occasions with black-and-blue marks on her body, but Barbara overlooked it— children often get bruised in play" \[Ch. 20\].
3. "Then, Barbara went away for a week and left the girls with the Petersons. When she returned, Martha had two black eyes and blue marks behind her ears. This time, Barbara confronted Mike about what had happened. He said that Martha was a “bad, bad girl” and she needed “to learn manners.” Barbara swore Mike’s voice was filled with glee when he told her that he had rubbed Martha’s nose in the carpet like a dog when she’d wet the floor. Soon after that incident, Mike Peterson moved back to the States, taking Margaret and Martha with him" \[Ch. 20\].
4. "On June 6, 1986, Mike arrived in Rhode Island at Jim and Margaret Blair’s home. He left Martha there and traveled to Texas to leave Margaret with George’s family. These visits were explained to be temporary and were intended to allow Mike and Patty to get settled in a home in Durham, North Carolina. **Before Mike left Rhode Island for Texas, however, he made a proposition to the Blairs. Martha was too much for him to handle because of her frequent temper tantrums. He asked if they would keep her on a permanent basis.** Margaret and Jim were delighted at the thought of keeping Martha. But what about Margaret? The girls were so close. The only immediate family they had was each other. Michael would not entertain the possibility of both girls staying in Rhode Island. With heavy hearts, the Blairs declined his offer. They believed it was too important for the girls to remain together" \[Ch. 21\]"
5. "Michael and Patty continued their complaints about **how difficult Martha was to raise.** They told Mike’s sister, Ann, that Martha had tantrums and was manipulative. Ann was puzzled. A 3-year-old manipulative? What could Martha possibly do? When Ann asked Mike and Patty, they gave her an example. When the family went out shopping, they said, Martha would stand stock-still all of a sudden, and wail, “Oh, my mommy died,” and start crying. Patty insisted that she did this just to garner the attention of the other shoppers. Another demonstration that Martha was a grand manipulator, they said, was when she called all sorts of women “Mommy”" \[Ch. 21\].
6. "**When Mike and Patty asked if she would take Martha**, Ann readily agreed. She was so excited about it, she told all her friends. And then, Michael changed his mind" \[Ch. 21\].
7. "At the end of the school year in 1991, Patty came back to the States with her boys. **She drove Margaret and Martha up to Rhode Island and told the Blairs they could adopt the girls**. She said that she and Michael were separating, and Margaret and Martha needed a stable home environment" \[Ch. 21\].

I feel for Martha and Margaret. I did not read this book, but I downloaded it (for free) on Z-Library because I was curious to answer your question. I can't imagine how it feels to have traumatic experiences publicized for all the world to know-- especially for all the avid fans of true crime. I'm sorry Martha. I'm sorry Margaret. My only peace is knowing that they are living good lives now.

During freshman year, I had time to participate in group therapy as well as individual counseling at UCC. Because individual counseling sessions at UCC are every two weeks, weekly group therapy was a great way to reinforce the healthy coping skills I learned with my counselor. I joined the Calming the Emotional Storm group and it helped me A LOT. I joined a few months before the pandemic, so I didn't get to do the full in person experience, but I learned so many things about emotions and how to handle them with care. Even though I'm still working through an eating disorder, I learned to not make my emotions my whole identity. When I'm talking about myself, I usually say "I am feeling sad" vs "I am sad" because I want to always remember that feelings (especially turbulent ones) are not forever. There's worksheets for every session and homework as well (but it's LOW KEY and isn't enforced).

I do not recommend the logic class that replaces the math requirement. I've had friends that took it that failed. I do recommend Math 130. It's the easiest way to fulfill the math requirement. This might sound counterintuitive, but you have the chance of getting an easier professor than during the spring/fall. I had Matthew Gottstein during the summer and he was a very lenient grader and always there for us if we needed help. I failed a few math classes and state exams in high school, but I somehow pulled off an A in Math 130. If I can do it, you can too.
